context_blurb:
Why does a child look like his or her parents? The first real rules came from a monk. Between 1856 and 1863 Gregor Mendel grew and counted more than 28,000 pea plants in his abbey's garden in Brno, now in the Czech Republic. Those counts began genetics, the science of how traits are handed down.

Picture a blacksmith whose arms have grown powerful from years of hammering. His strength is an acquired trait, gained during his life. Strength built by work changes his muscles, not the genes he passes on, so his son inherits none of it. The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck taught that traits gained by use pass to the young; genetics found no way for that to happen. A child gets about half of his or her genes from each parent, but none of what a parent gains in life.

A pea flower pollinates itself, so a variety left alone breeds true. To choose a flower's father, Mendel had to stop that. Pollen is made by the anthers, at the tips of the stamens, and a pea's anthers burst inside the bud before it opens. So Mendel opened young buds and plucked out the anthers, the pollen makers, with fine forceps. The stigma, where pollen lands, and the ovary, where seeds form, were left in place. Then he dusted the stigma with pollen from the father plant he had chosen.

Mendel crossed pure tall plants with pure short ones. Most naturalists of the day expected blending, offspring halfway between their parents, like red and white paint stirred to pink. Instead, every plant of the first generation grew tall, and the short trait seemed to have vanished. Mendel called such a trait, one that shows in every hybrid, dominant. When he let those hybrids pollinate themselves, 787 plants of the second generation grew tall and 277 grew short. That is about three tall for every short one, so roughly one plant in four was short again. The short trait had only been hiding, and Mendel called a trait like that recessive.

Mendel explained this with separate hereditary factors, one from each parent, which the Danish botanist Wilhelm Johannsen named genes in 1909. Inside a tall hybrid, the tall factor and the short factor stay separate and unchanged, so the hybrid can pass its short factor on as whole as it came in. Blending could never explain that. We now call a gene's versions alleles. When a pea makes pollen or egg cells, each grain or egg gets just one of its two alleles for height, tall or short by chance.

One tall allele is enough to make a pea tall. So a pea with two tall alleles looks just like one with a tall and a short. The two share a phenotype, the trait that shows, but differ in genotype, the pair of alleles each carries. If two tall plants have a short seedling, each must carry one short allele, because a short plant needs one from both parents. A Punnett square, a grid pairing each parent's possible alleles, turns these rules into chances. Cross a hybrid with a short plant, and the short parent can give only short alleles. Two of the grid's four boxes then come out short-short, so about one half of the seeds should grow short. The famous one in four holds only for a cross of two hybrids, and the square gives chances, never an exact count.

Mendel read his paper to Brno's natural history society in 1865. Then the paper sat in a small society's journal, and few scientists took any notice of it, citing it only a handful of times before 1900. Even Charles Darwin seems never to have heard of it. Mendel died in 1884, and sixteen years later Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns, who had found the same patterns in their own crosses, brought his paper to light. Mendel is now called the father of modern genetics.
